content: Many medical abortion interventions, particularly those in early pregnancy, can now be effectively provided at the primary care level and on an outpatient basis, significantly improving access to care. Self-assessment and self-management approaches empower individuals and help prioritize care, optimizing the use of healthcare resources. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends self-management of medical abortion. Recommendations on Self-Care in Medical Abortion and Post-Abortion Contraception: 1. Self-assessment of eligibility for medical abortion is recommended within the framework of rigorous research. 2. Self-management of mifepristone and misoprostol without direct supervision of a healthcare worker is recommended in specific circumstances, provided individuals have access to accurate information and healthcare support if needed. 3. Self-assessment of abortion completeness using pregnancy tests and checklists is recommended in cases where mifepristone and misoprostol are used, with access to accurate information and healthcare support. 4. Self-administration of injectable contraceptives is recommended in contexts where appropriate training, information, and healthcare linkages are available. 5. For individuals undergoing medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol who desire hormonal contraception, it is suggested they be given the option to start contraception immediately after the first pill of the abortion regimen. Combating Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), Reproductive Tract Infections, and Cervical Cancer: STIs are among the most common communicable diseases, affecting the health of women, men, and infants globally. Annually, there are approximately 357 million new infections of four curable STIs: chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and trichomoniasis. Many STIs, including HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B, can also be transmitted from mother to child during pregnancy and childbirth. WHO recommends self-collection of samples for testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Treponema pallidum (syphilis), and Trichomonas vaginalis as additional approaches to STI testing services. HIV Prevention and Testing: HIV attacks the immune system, specifically CD4 cells. It can be diagnosed using simple and affordable rapid diagnostic tests, and WHO recommends HIV self-testing. HIV testing services should adhere to the five Cs: consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct results, and connection to treatment and services. Cervical Cancer: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women, with an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths worldwide in 2020. Nearly all cases (99%) are linked to high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, a virus transmitted through sexual contact. Effective prevention through HPV vaccination and screening for precancerous lesions can prevent most cases. When detected early, cervical cancer is one of the most treatable cancers. Recommendations for HPV and STI Testing: 1. HPV self-sampling should be available as an additional approach for cervical cancer screening in individuals aged 30–60 years. 2. Self-collection of samples for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis should be available as an additional approach for STI testing. 3. Self-collection of samples for Treponema pallidum (syphilis) and Trichomonas vaginalis may be considered as an additional approach for STI testing. 4. HIV self-testing should be offered as an additional approach to HIV testing services. Promoting Sexual Health: Sexual health is defined as a state of physical, emotional, mental, and social well-being in relation to sexuality. It requires a positive and respectful approach to sexuality and sexual relationships, as well as the possibility of pleasurable and safe sexual experiences free of coercion, discrimination, and violence. Achieving sexual health depends on access to comprehensive, high-quality information about sex and sexuality, knowledge of risks, access to sexual healthcare, and an environment that affirms and promotes sexual health. Self-Care After Sexual Assault or Violence: Survivors of sexual assault should be provided with detailed explanations of examination findings, treatment options, and follow-up care. They should be educated on wound care, signs of infection, and the importance of completing prescribed medications. Follow-up visits should be planned at regular intervals to monitor recovery and address any ongoing concerns. Use of Lubricants for Sexual Health: The use of lubricants during sexual activity can improve sexual health and well-being, particularly for individuals experiencing vaginal dryness, dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), or engaging in anal sex. WHO recommends making lubricants available for optional use during sexual activity. Evidence suggests that lubricants can enhance sexual satisfaction and reduce discomfort, with no significant adverse effects reported. WHO recommends offering oral PrEP and the dapivirine vaginal ring to individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection. Equitable access to PrEP is essential to improve uptake, particularly among underserved populations.
